 News Elections Sport Entertainment Opinion Consumer S Mag Hot Topics Listen Motoring Careers Podcasts Partners News EXPLAINER | What to do when the manufacturer recalls your faulty car
 Motorists have been urged to take vehicle recalls seriously and return affected cars for repairs
 November 13, 2026 at 4:00 pm 3 min read 
 Share current article via Email Share current article via Facebook Share current article via Twitter Share current article via LinkedIn Nandi Ntini
 Social Justice News Reporter
 Opens in new window Opens in new window Opens in new window Opens in new window Enter fullscreen mode displaying this image. Expand The National Consumer Commission announced a recall involving 738 Volvo EX30 and EX30 Cross Country vehicles covering certain 2024 to 2027 models. Picture: Supplied 
 Story audio is generated using AI 
 Motorists have been urged to take vehicle recalls seriously and return affected cars for repairs as the National Consumer Commission (NCC) warns that driving vehicles with known safety defects could put lives at risk.
 The warning comes amid a growing number of vehicle recalls this year, with thousands of cars affected by safety concerns involving different manufacturers.
 The latest recall this week involves 23,667 Chery Tiggo 4, Omoda C5 and Chery Tiggo 8 Pro Max 2.0 vehicles following a notification by Chery International, trading as Chery South Africa.
 Also, this week the NCC announced a separate recall involving 738 Volvo EX30 and EX30 Cross Country vehicles covering certain 2024 to 2027 models.
 NCC spokesperson Phetho Ntaba said motorists whose vehicles are affected should follow the manufacturer’s instructions and ensure that the necessary corrective work is carried out.
 “What is imperative is for consumers to heed the call and return recalled vehicles, as continuous usage poses further risks,” she said.
 Motorists should first establish whether their vehicles are affected by checking the recall notice and contacting the manufacturer or dealership.
 They should then follow the instructions provided, including arranging an inspection or repair where required. They should not assume that a vehicle is safe to drive simply because it has not shown any symptoms of the reported defect.
 What is imperative is for consumers to heed the call and return recalled vehicles, as continuous usage poses further risks
 —   Phetho Ntaba, NCC spokesperson Ntaba said the time needed to repair a recalled vehicle depended on the nature of the defect and the availability of replacement parts.
 This means motorists may have to wait for parts or repairs to be completed. However, they should not continue using a vehicle if the manufacturer or recall notice advises against it.
 Importantly, she said motorists who are still paying instalments on their vehicles are not exempt from recalls. The financial commitment does not remove the safety risk or the need to have the defect addressed.
 Consumers experiencing difficulties during the recall process can contact the NCC at productrecall@thencc.org.za.
 Ntaba said consumers did not need to lodge formal complaints with the commission simply because their vehicles had been recalled. They should first follow the manufacturer’s recall instructions.
 However, the NCC has powers to intervene when manufacturers or suppliers fail to disclose safety concerns or do not properly inform affected consumers.
 Ntaba said the Consumer Protection Act (CPA) requires that suppliers notify the commission within two days of becoming aware of a safety concern.
 Manufacturers must also take reasonable steps to inform affected vehicle owners about the risks and explain what action they need to take.
 Ntaba said the commission could investigate manufacturers and suppliers whose conduct was inconsistent with the act.
 It could also compel manufacturers to investigate safety concerns and take corrective measures, including recalling affected vehicles.
 Section 60 of the CPA provides that unsafe goods must be recalled for repairs, replacement or refunds.
 The commission has also raised concern about suppliers who allegedly conceal recalls or fail to notify it about safety problems.
 “There are instances where suppliers hide recalls or do not notify the NCC for reasons unknown to the NCC,” Ntaba said.
 “Where recalls were not communicated on time or not communicated at all, the NCC is investigating such matters.”
 Manufacturers who fail to comply with the CPA could face enforcement action, including referral to the National Consumer Tribunal.
 The tribunal has the power to impose administrative fines of up to 10% of a supplier’s annual turnover.
 Figures published by Top Auto in June showed that the NCC had issued 17 vehicle recall notices affecting 39,164 vehicles since the beginning of the year.
 The growing number of recalls highlights the importance of motorists paying attention to safety notices and manufacturers being transparent about defects that could endanger road users.
